message.abstract: <jats:p>Road defect detection often uses supervised trained deep learning models that suffer from low reliability in different road scenes. While synthetic data augmentation has been widely used to address data scarcity, its effectiveness is typically evaluated only through downstream task performance in the same context, with little analysis interpreting how synthetic data affects the internal representations and spatial attention of detection models. This paper identifies data scarcity and context variation as two distinct deficiencies in defect detection. Experiments proceed by procedurally adding potholes synthesised from baseline pavement images and images from external sources, and examine if they address both deficiencies. To further illustrate the effects, the trained models were evaluated on test sets within and beyond the training context, using interpretation techniques such as logistic regression probes, EigenCAM heatmaps and bounding box (bbox) inspectors to help explain the root causes of improvements or failures. Results suggested that synthesising instances onto a target background improves detection on that background by improving both classification and localisation. When evaluating across contexts, however, a diagnosis of poor detection suggests that classification tend to generalise more effectively than spatial attention. Diffused spatial attention hinders the differentiation of background and foreground and creates a localisation bottleneck. These findings suggest that robustness in real-world applications depends on exposure to diverse image backgrounds and a strategic integration of synthetic data from multiple sources.</jats:p>
title: Cross-Context Synthetic Data for Road Defect Detection: An Interpretability Analysis
